contexts.summary: Tyrol's present Austrian territory consists of North Tyrol and East Tyrol. The division of historic Tyrol after the First World War left South Tyrol in Italy; Innsbruck is the capital.
The Kaisergebirge comprises the Wilder Kaiser and Zahmer Kaiser limestone massifs, between Kufstein and St. Johann in Tirol.
The historical reference reports medieval name forms associated with Baumburg Abbey, with dates given as ranges rather than a single secure founding year.
Upper Austria developed from the territory north of the Enns, separated from Styria in the medieval period. Linz is the regional capital.
The Salzkammergut mountains combine limestone ranges with the flysch foothills of Salzburg and Upper Austria.
Steinbach's parish church is documented in 1276; its own parish chronicle begins in 1781.
The Dachstein massif spans Upper Austria, Salzburg and Styria. Its limestone karst, caves and the salt-mining heritage around Hallstatt provide distinct natural and cultural history.
Gosau is documented in 1231. Its early history includes conflict over salt production, including destruction of a saltworks in 1295.
Styria became a duchy in 1180. Its historical territory was divided after the First World War; Graz is the capital of today's Austrian state.
The Ennstal Alps contain the Gesäuse, where the Enns cuts through limestone mountains near Admont.
Admont is documented in 859, and its abbey was founded in 1074. The town and church were affected by the fire of 1865.

Carinthia is Austria's southernmost state, centred on Klagenfurt. Its history combines alpine settlement, medieval territorial rule and the border between German-speaking and Slovene-speaking communities.
The Schober group was distinguished as a separate mountain group in nineteenth-century Alpine classifications. Petzeck is its highest summit.
Großkirchheim castle is documented around 1140–1150. Gold and other precious-metal mining shaped the surrounding Hohe Tauern economy.
The Upper Austrian Prealps occupy the foothill country between the Traun, Enns and Steyr, linking alpine valleys with the northern foreland.
Bad Goisern appears in a medieval register around 1325 under an earlier name. Its history belongs to the salt-producing Salzkammergut.
Germany's modern history includes the foundation of the Federal Republic in 1949 and reunification in 1990. The listed German huts belong to several distinct regional landscapes.
The Bavarian Prealps are limestone mountains extending across the German-Austrian border.
Bavaria's monarchy ended in 1918, when it became a free state. Munich is its capital; the Bavarian Alps share longstanding cultural and transport links with Tyrol and Salzburg.
Salzburg was governed for centuries by prince-archbishops before secularisation. It became part of Austria in 1816.
The Ankogel group's name and boundaries developed through nineteenth-century Alpine classification. The Hochalmspitze is its highest mountain.
The Großarl valley is documented around 930. Salzburg's archbishops became major landholders around 1000.
The Villgraten mountains were classified and renamed during the nineteenth century; they are also associated with the Defereggen name.
The settlement history of Villgraten includes forest clearance authorised by Innichen Abbey in 1140. The much earlier valley reference comes from a later-altered document.
Gastein is documented in 963. Thermal bathing and mining shaped Bad Gastein; Austria and Prussia signed the Gastein Convention here in 1865.
The Carnic Alps follow the Austrian-Italian border. Their Paleozoic rocks and ancient reef deposits provide an unusually long geological record.
The Totes Gebirge is a limestone and karst plateau range in Styria and Upper Austria, with the Großer Priel among its prominent summits.
Medieval records link the Alm valley's fishing and pasture rights with Lambach Abbey. The abbey's foundation in 1056 is part of this regional history.
The ranges east of the Mur form the eastern margin of the Alps. This broad group covers several local landscapes rather than a single historical settlement region.
The Plöckenpass carried a Roman route. Archaeological finds and later trade over the pass form part of Kötschach-Mauthen's historical context.
Roman Brigantium, today's Bregenz, was part of Raetia. Alemannic settlement later shaped Vorarlberg, Austria's westernmost state.
The Lechquellen mountains in Vorarlberg encompass the headwaters of the Lech and extend towards the Großes Walsertal.
Sonntag had a parish by 1457. Buchboden became an independent parish in 1710.
Mallnitz is documented in 1299. Its high valley was connected with trade across the Tauern passes.
The Lesach valley's settlement history includes Bavarian settlers arriving from the west and the development of livestock farms by around 1300.
The Kitzbühel Alps belong largely to the greywacke zone. Schist, phyllite and ancient volcanic rocks shape their softer mountain forms.
Lower Austria's history is linked to the medieval Ostarrichi territory, documented in 996. The modern state surrounds Vienna and includes the eastern Alpine foothills.
The Wetterstein range straddles Bavaria and Tyrol and includes the Zugspitze. Triassic limestone is central to its geological character.
The Mieming range in Tyrol contains rocks deposited during the Triassic and Jurassic periods.
Telfs has archaeological evidence from the Iron Age and Roman period. It later became an important transport, judicial and administrative centre.
The Leutasch river area is documented in a donation of 1177. This records the landscape rather than a precise village founding date.
The Berchtesgaden Alps include the Watzmann and Hochkönig. Thick limestone and dolomite strata shape their cliffs and plateaus.
The Allgäu Alps cross Bavaria, Tyrol and Vorarlberg, east of Lake Constance. Their boundary landscape includes Germany's southernmost point.
The Stubai Alps lie southwest of Innsbruck and extend towards the Brenner and northern Italy. Their natural history includes ancient metamorphic rocks and local mining.
The Maria Hilf chapel was built in 1655 and expanded in 1703. Its devotional image made Gries a pilgrimage destination.
The Ybbstal Alps lie in the Eisenwurzen border region of Lower Austria, Upper Austria and Styria.
Gaflenz has belonged to the territory of Upper Austria since 1490. Its local history includes fighting during the Ottoman advance of 1529.
Opponitz is recorded in 1256. Vienna built the local hydroelectric power station between 1922 and 1924.
The Lechtal Alps are a limestone range in western Tyrol and eastern Vorarlberg. The Parseierspitze is the group's highest summit.
Namlos is documented in 1286. Its early settlement involved forest clearance and livestock farming.
The Türnitz Alps are a Lower Austrian and Styrian foothill range; the Sulzberg is its highest mountain.
Annaberg's settlement developed from land granted to Lilienfeld Abbey in 1202; the abbey established farming and religious buildings on the pass.
Schnann is documented in 1275. Its first church building was completed in 1646.
Flirsch's present centre, Persir, is documented in 1275; the village name appears in a register of 1358.
Kufstein's area has prehistoric finds in the Tischofer cave. The town is documented around 788–790, and its strategically important fortress in 1205.
The Ötztal Alps extend across the Austrian-Italian border. Their high alpine landscape includes glaciers and long-used routes across the main Alpine divide.
Ried is documented between 1115 and 1122. Sigmundsried castle later became an administrative and judicial centre.
Losenstein castle was built around 1150; the place is documented in 1170. Its history is linked with the medieval Otakar and Babenberg territories.
Baden-Württemberg contains the Black Forest and Swabian Jura, with distinct Baden and Württemberg traditions. The linked regional history explains the territories that formed the modern state.
Buchen is documented in 773–774 in the Lorsch Codex. Earlier finds show prehistoric and Roman occupation.
Mittenwald lay on the Roman Via Raetia. Medieval settlement and trade developed around the route; the town received market rights in 1305.
The Samnaun group crosses Tyrol and Graubünden. Modern ski development is a notable part of its more recent landscape history.
See in Paznaun is named in a document of 1433; earlier tax registers record the surrounding area.
The Karwendel spans Tyrol and Bavaria. Folded limestone forms steep north faces and glacial cirques.
Grins is documented in 1288. In 1330, the Tyrolean ruler directed the Arlberg road through the village.
The Ammergau Alps extend across Upper Bavaria, Swabia and the Reutte area of Tyrol.
Unterammergau is documented in 1280. It remained connected with Ettal Abbey's territories until secularisation in 1803.
Ramsau is documented around 1120. From 1599 to 1781, local Protestant belief had to be practised privately.
Ellmau is documented between 1153 and 1156. Its position on the Salzburg–Innsbruck route led to a postal station around 1616.
The Venediger group belongs to the Hohe Tauern and is associated with the Großvenediger and its glaciated high mountain landscape.
The Rieserferner group crosses Italy and Austria. Glaciers and high mountain basins are central to its character.
Saxony-Anhalt's historical regions include the former Prussian province of Saxony and Anhalt. Magdeburg is its capital.
Schierke's earliest records, from 1588–1591, concern a sawmill on the Kalte Bode.
The Brandenberg Alps include the Rofan, between the Achensee and the Inn valley.
Münster is documented in 1257, while its parish origins are considerably older.

Vintl's surrounding heritage includes stone quarrying in Pfunders, with local green marble extracted from 1722.
Bad Tabarz's surrounding landscape contains medieval castle sites, including Torstein above the Lauchagrund.
Krakauschatten became an autonomous municipality in 1850 after the abolition of manorial rule.
Königssee is a lake and historic visitor landscape rather than a town. Its linked reference provides geographical and cultural context.
Weerberg appears in a record of 1285. A Tyrolean tax register of 1312 recorded its population.
Floh and Seligenthal developed from older forest villages and were recorded by the Henneberg counts in the fourteenth century.
Weißbriach's church is documented in 1331. The Reformation later had a strong influence on the local community.
The Mönichwald area has prehistoric finds from the Lafnitz valley, preceding the later settlement and parish history.
Arborn is documented in 1391 in a grant involving the Essershausen estate and rights in surrounding settlements.
Bühlertal is documented in 1301. It came fully under Baden's rule in 1688.
Fieberbrunn is documented in 1156 under an earlier name. Mining contributed to its later prosperity.
Winklern is documented between 1041 and 1060, while nearby Penzelberg has earlier records. Its toll tower is a separate historical feature.
Langenbach near Kirburg is documented in 1261.
Lermoos is documented between 1073 and 1078. The Roman Via Claudia Augusta crossed the area.
Wolfsberg's area has prehistoric and Roman finds. Its castle is documented in 1178; this is a castle date rather than the town's foundation.
Würgau has medieval records and longstanding links with Langheim Abbey. It became part of Scheßlitz in 1978.
Oberweißenbrunn's recorded local history begins around 1500. Its earlier churches were replaced by the present building in 1961.
Vorderstoder's systematic forest clearance began around 1170. Two surviving church bells date from 1401.
Grödig is documented in 790. Its name has several proposed interpretations associated with the local rock landscape.
Obdach is documented in 1190. It received market rights in 1324; the modern municipality was created in 1849–1850.
Rauris is documented in 1120. Earlier finds attest to travel across its Tauern routes, while gold mining shaped later regional history.

sources.name: Otto-Haus
sources.title: Ottohaus operator visit information
sources.use: Season starts 1 May 2026; summer overnights daily. About 30 minutes from cable-car upper station. Vegetarian/vegan dishes advertised. Exact closing date not established.

sources.name: Otto-Haus
sources.title: Ottohaus rooms and prices 2026
sources.use: Double room from EUR 59/person; single-use supplement EUR 20/night. Breakfast/bedding/towels included; shared washrooms, no heating or room sockets; dining-room charging/Wi-Fi. Pet and climate fees separate.

sources.title: Sektion Reichenau newsletter 91, printed p. 12

sources.name: Franz-Fischer-Hütte
sources.title: Franz-Fischer building and capacity account
sources.use: Present timber hut built in 2013; later building, not original opening. Operator: 23 room, 12 dormitory, 10 emergency places. Directory winter/emergency categories differ.

sources.name: Franz-Fischer-Hütte
sources.title: Franz-Fischer booking and operating dates
sources.use: Staffed season 4 June–4 October 2026. All stays require booking. Cash only; check-in 15:00, checkout 09:00, dinner 18:30, quiet 22:00. Old availability snippets are not live availability.

sources.name: Franz-Fischer-Hütte
sources.title: Franz-Fischer road access and approaches
sources.use: Car toll/parking EUR 12; 2026 holiday-period road restriction/shuttle dates. Road page gives a provisional 11 July–13 September 2026 shuttle period with an unfinished 2026 timetable and mixed 2025 blocks. Overnight parking duration unstated.

sources.name: Franz-Fischer-Hütte
sources.title: Franz-Fischer shortest published approach
sources.use: From upper hut car park via access road: about 450 m ascent; published 45-minute runner time to 1.5 hours, experienced hikers about 1 hour. Access road closed to vehicles including mountain bikes. Page dated 18 March 2024; route estimate, not a current condition guarantee.

sources.name: Franz-Fischer-Hütte
sources.title: Franz-Fischer approach via Jakoberalm
sources.use: Published 3-hour approach from Schliereralm via Jakoberalm and Essersee on Centralalpenweg 02. Page dated 18 March 2024; route estimate, not current condition guarantee.

sources.name: Franz-Fischer-Hütte
sources.title: Franz-Fischer summer 2026 tariffs, p. 1
sources.use: Adult room/dormitory rates, separate meal-package age bands, dog fee. German ab 16 versus English >16; age bands overlap at 6/16. Keep labels and confirm boundaries.

sources.name: Franz-Fischer-Hütte
sources.title: Franz-Fischer 2026 visitor information, pp. 1–2
sources.use: Vegetarian/vegan meals. Advance-notice accommodation of lactose/gluten/nut intolerance; other allergies not catered for under posted policy. Liner required, dogs leashed, cash/quiet 22:00; EUR 35/person/night cancellation inside 7 days.
sources.date_qualification: Linked as 2026 rules; upload path not revision date

sources.name: Bielefelder Hütte

sources.title: Alplhaus history by Horst Höfler
sources.use: Predecessor summer residence built 1865, section acquired it in 1890, destroyed in 1921. Account dates present building completion to 1925, conflicting with Wikipedia infobox replacement 1924. Separate renovation reopening 14 October 2018.

sources.name: Alplhaus
sources.title: Alplhaus equipment and stays
sources.use: Self-catering, reservation arrangement, 16 listed places. No pets, no smoking or campfires, quiet 23:00, no running water, drinking source 10–15 minutes away. Current property page does not establish a universal key entitlement.

sources.title: DAV Mannheim: Oberzalimhütte
sources.use: 2007 renovation and 2017 environmental award after photovoltaic installation; original construction date remains unresolved. Brand via Glinga/Fürggelesteig about three hours; bicycle access prohibited by landowners. Intermediary stop toward Mannheimer Hütte.

sources.name: Oberzalimhütte
sources.title: Oberzalimhütte dated news
sources.use: Notice dated 8 September: hut closed from 30 September 2026; summer 2027 reservations available from early 2027. The 28 June 2026 Leibersteig work notice is historical and does not establish today's route conditions.

sources.name: Oberzalimhütte

sources.name: Brünnsteinhaus

November/December programme has gaps and must not be extrapolated.

film_formats.proposal: Approach shot, one sourced historical fact, a brief hut portrait and a published approach-time overlay.
film_formats.qualification: Choose a historical date with its confidence and source. Keep overlays tied to the named start point.

film_formats.proposal: Follow a load from valley to hut and connect the landscape with the people doing the work.
film_formats.qualification: Historical supply cableway relationship is secondary. Present logistics, delivery dates, route access and filming consent remain unconfirmed.

film_formats.proposal: Use ground-level exterior and shelter details to explain a 1971 emergency bivouac.
film_formats.qualification: Emergency shelter with two benches; ordinary beds not listed. Do not stage an unnecessary overnight or infer flight clearance.

film_formats.format: From the 1922 predecessor to the 1954 hut
film_formats.proposal: Contrast the predecessor inauguration with the present replacement building using cleared archival material.
film_formats.qualification: 1922 is the predecessor. Current building opened 4 August 1954.

film_formats.proposal: Explain the self-catering routine after arranging authorized access with the section.
film_formats.qualification: Current key procedure unconfirmed. Present completion 1925 conflicts with secondary 1924 replacement date.

film_formats.proposal: A restrained account of place and remembrance, only if the organizers and participants agree.
film_formats.qualification: Scheduled 17 October 2026, 11:00. Occurrence and filming consent unconfirmed. Water/booking and operator-change notices affect a visit.

film_formats.proposal: Approach at dawn, staff routine, arrivals, a meal and an evening exterior; night sequence only after access and scouting.
film_formats.qualification: Operator/interview/kitchen consent required. Staffed 2026 seasons ended; Hohenzollern winter blockhouse is separate.

film_formats.proposal: Repeat authorized ground viewpoints through winter, spring, summer and autumn.
film_formats.qualification: Winter access is not guaranteed. Oberzalim closed from 30 September 2026; 2027 booking opening is not a season date.

film_formats.proposal: Select four inventory huts in one range and connect their stories through the landscape.
film_formats.qualification: Select by recorded mountain group. Travel/approach times and permissions need individual planning.

film_formats.proposal: Compare founding, interwar, post-war and 1970s building stories using verified dates and cleared archives.
film_formats.qualification: Requisitions, destruction and ownership transfers need hut-specific evidence; organizational dates cannot be generalized to every hut.

film_formats.format: People, kitchens and the sound of a hut
film_formats.proposal: Portraits, a kitchen routine, meal preparation and ambient sound at agreed times.
film_formats.qualification: Interview, interior, kitchen and participant consent remain separate personal permission records.

film_formats.proposal: Record a clear horizon or seasonal change from a repeatable ground spot after scouting.
film_formats.qualification: Sky exposure, night access, horizon, moon, weather and light pollution are unconfirmed until scouted.

film_formats.proposal: Identify images or testimony that support the date and place, then document attribution and rights.
film_formats.qualification: Historic does not imply public domain. Record licence, rights holder or permission before reuse.

film_formats.proposal: Consider an exterior reveal or short route segment only within permitted flight limits.
film_formats.qualification: No flight permission or airspace clearance recorded. A full valley-to-hut route may exceed permitted operating limits; check date, zones, protected-area rules and category before planning.
